content: The left lung is anatomically divided into two lobes: the upper lobe and the lower lobe. These lobes are separated by the oblique fissure, which extends from the costal surface to the mediastinal surface of the lung, both above and below the hilum. On the surface of the lung, the oblique fissure originates on the mediastinal surface at the upper and posterior part of the hilum. It then runs backward and upward to cross the posterior border of the lung at a point approximately 6 cm below the apex. From there, the fissure extends downward and forward across the costal surface, reaching the lower border slightly behind the anterior extremity of the lung. Its course can then be traced upward and backward across the mediastinal surface, terminating at the lower part of the hilum. The superior lobe of the left lung is located above and in front of the oblique fissure. It includes the apex of the lung, the anterior border, a significant portion of the costal surface, and the majority of the mediastinal surface. The inferior lobe, which is larger than the superior lobe, is situated below and behind the oblique fissure. It encompasses nearly the entire base of the lung, a large portion of the costal surface, and most of the posterior border. On the mediastinal surface of the left lung, immediately above the hilum, there is a prominent curved groove created by the aortic arch. Extending upward from this groove toward the apex of the lung is a channel accommodating the left subclavian artery. An additional slight impression in front of this groove, near the margin of the lung, houses the left innominate vein. Behind the hilum and the pulmonary ligament, a vertical groove is formed by the descending aorta. In front of this groove, near the base of the lung, the lower part of the esophagus creates a shallow impression. Additional anatomical images and diagrams provide further context for understanding the respiratory system. These include depictions of the anatomy of the lungs, a frontal view of the heart and lungs, a transverse section of the thorax showing the relationship of the pulmonary artery, the position and relationship of the esophagus in the cervical region and posterior mediastinum (as seen from behind), and the thymus gland of a full-term fetus exposed in situ.
